lesson_title: Round Up or Round Down? The Question That Decides the Mark
hook_text: 8,99 litres of paint means buy 10. 5,99 days of water means you get 5. Almost the same decimal, opposite answers.
clip_script: Here is what nobody tells you about measurement questions: the maths is the easy half. The last step decides the mark. Painting the spare room, you work it out and you need 8,99 litres. Do you buy 8? Never — you go UP. You cannot buy 0,99 of a tin, and coming home short means a second taxi trip and a wall in two shades. Now the water tank. It holds 2 036 litres, the family of four uses 340 a day, so 2 036 divided by 340 is 5,99 days. Surely that rounds to 6? No — you go DOWN. Even at five point nine nine. The sixth day runs dry a few litres before supper, so the family gets five full days, and writing six promises them water that is not there. Nearly the same decimal, opposite decisions. So the rule was never about the number — it is about the situation. Materials round UP, because you must have enough. Days and whole items round DOWN, because a part of one does not count. Ask which kind you are holding, every single time. That is the mark.
visual_style: Split screen: a paint tin filling past an 8,99 line and clicking up to 10 with an up arrow, against a water tank draining across five full sunrises and dying just before the sixth, with a down arrow.
mood: Practical, slightly conspiratorial — the tip nobody gave you.
pacing: Quick hook, two clean contrasting beats, firm rule at the close.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson for fencing, tiling and tank calculations in rands.
